chapters.name: Table
learn: Ratio of two values, or of two row or column totals
Percentage by which one sum exceeds or is less than another; one value as a percentage of a total
Average of a row or column; count the entries above the average
Year with the highest percentage increase over the previous year
Convert a table value into a pie-chart central angle (value ÷ total × 360°)
Marks tables: convert to percentage and count students above a cut-off
Cumulative ("less than") frequency tables: read class frequencies and counts below a cut-off
chapters.note: The most common data-interpretation format; usually a set of several questions on one table.

chapters.name: Line Graph
learn: Difference between two values read from the graph
Percentage by which one value exceeds another
Year showing a rise over the previous year
Total over several years multiplied by a per-unit amount
chapters.note: Rare: one set in a single CHSL paper.

chapters.name: Algebraic Identities
learn: From x + 1/x (or x − 1/x) find x² + 1/x², x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k, x⁴ + 1/x⁴, and up to the 5th and 6th powers
Work backwards: from x² + 1/x² or x⁴ + 1/x⁴ get x + 1/x; divide a quadratic by x to reach the x + 1/x form
Special cases: x + 1/x = 2 gives x = 1; x + 1/x = −2 gives x = −1
a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) and a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), often with comparing coefficients
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca); if a + b + c = 0 then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca); a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab; (a + b)² − (a − b)² = 4ab
A sum of squares equal to zero makes every term zero; a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca gives a = b = c
Surd inputs: rationalise, or write 3 + 2√2 as a perfect square, before applying the identity
chapters.note: The most repeated maths chapter: in almost every paper, often two questions.

chapters.name: Linear and Quadratic Equations
learn: Form and solve one or two linear equations from a word problem (coins and notes, heads and legs, two-digit numbers)
Solve a quadratic, often from a number and its reciprocal, then evaluate a related expression
Equations with square roots: square both sides or substitute the options
Sum of roots = −b/a; equal roots when b² − 4ac = 0
Pair of linear equations has infinitely many solutions when a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂
Solve two linear inequalities and pick a value in the common range (CHSL)
nth term of an arithmetic progression from two given terms (asked once)

chapters.name: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
learn: Equilateral triangle: area = (√3/4) × side²; rhombus: ½ × product of diagonals; trapezium: ½ × sum of parallel sides × height
Square and rectangle: area from perimeter or diagonal, sides from perimeter and area, paths around a field, number of tiles
Circle: circumference 2πr, area πr², areas in the ratio of the squares of radii, ring between concentric circles
Sector: arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr; area = (θ/360) × πr² = ½ × radius × arc; perimeter = arc + 2r
Percentage change in area when the sides or the radius change by given percentages (a + b + ab/100)
Wheel revolutions = distance ÷ circumference
chapters.note: The most asked part of mensuration.

chapters.name: Cylinder
learn: Curved surface area 2πrh, total surface area 2πr(r + h), volume πr²h
Find volume from curved surface area and base area, or height and radius from one another
Ratio of volumes or curved surfaces from ratios of radii and heights
Hollow cylinder (pipe, road roller): volume and weight of material
Rise in water level when a sphere is immersed; filling a cuboid from a cylinder
chapters.note: The most asked solid.

chapters.name: Combined and Recast Solids
learn: Melting and recasting: equate volumes, then find a dimension, a surface area or the number of pieces
Surface area of a combined solid (a frustum topped by a hemisphere, a cube with hemispherical depressions)
Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 for polyhedra
chapters.note: Rare, but the equate-the-volumes idea also runs through the cylinder and sphere chapters.

chapters.name: Sphere and Hemisphere
learn: Sphere: volume (4/3)πr³, surface area 4πr²; find the radius from one and compute the other
Hemisphere: curved surface area 2πr², total surface area 3πr²; cutting a sphere in half adds two circular faces
Hollow sphere: volume = (4/3)π(R³ − r³)
Number of small spheres from a melted sphere or cylinder = ratio of volumes
Largest sphere inside a cube has diameter equal to the side; water-level rise when a sphere is dropped in a cylinder

chapters.name: Trigonometric Ratios and Standard Angles
learn: Evaluate an expression using the values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Given one ratio (tan θ, cot θ, cosec θ), find the others from a right triangle and evaluate an expression; divide through by cos θ to use tan θ
Solve a simple equation for the angle, then evaluate; equations that reduce to a quadratic in sin, cos or tan
Find A and B from standard values of sin(A + B) and cos(A − B)
Complementary pairs: tan A = cot B when A + B = 90°
Angles beyond 90°: quadrant signs, negative angles, periodicity (mainly CHSL and 2023)
Cosine rule for the third side (asked once)
chapters.note: With identities, this gives two or three trigonometry questions in most papers.

chapters.name: Trigonometric Identities
learn: sin² + cos² = 1, sec² − tan² = 1, cosec² − cot² = 1, used to simplify long expressions
Reciprocal trick: sec θ − tan θ = 1/(sec θ + tan θ), and the same for cosec θ and cot θ
Root forms: √((1 − sin)/(1 + sin)) = sec − tan; √((1 + cos)/(1 − cos)) = cosec + cot
Higher powers: sin⁴ + cos⁴ = 1 − 2sin²cos², sin⁶ + cos⁶ = 1 − 3sin²cos², tan² + cot² + 2 = sec² cosec²
Complementary angles: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, so cos²θ + cos²(90° − θ) = 1 and cot θ × cot(90° − θ) = 1
Double and triple angles: tan 2θ, (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ) = tan²θ, cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ
Squaring and adding two linear sin-cos equations; if A + B = 45° then (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2
Sum-to-product formulas (sin C + sin D) and maximum or minimum values (tan² + cot² ≥ 2)
chapters.note: Asked in most papers, often two questions.

chapters.name: Coordinate Geometry
learn: Section formula and mid-point formula (including finding an end point)
Slope of a line through two points; slope of a perpendicular is the negative reciprocal
Equation of a line from a point and a slope or inclination (slope = tan θ); intercepts
Reflection of a point in the lines x = k or y = k
chapters.note: Asked only in 2017 papers (CGL and CHSL); it has not appeared in this set since.

chapters.name: Similar Triangles
learn: Ratio of areas of similar triangles = square of the ratio of corresponding sides (also altitudes, medians, perimeters)
Basic proportionality theorem: a line parallel to the base divides the sides in the same ratio, DE/BC = AD/AB
Sides of similar triangles are in the ratio of their perimeters
AA similarity in triangles sharing an angle, giving results like CA² = CD × CB
Altitude on the hypotenuse: BD² = AD × CD and AB² = AD × AC
Converse of the basic proportionality theorem; applying the theorem twice with two parallel lines
chapters.note: The area-ratio result is asked again and again.

chapters.name: Quadrilaterals
learn: Angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°
Properties of a parallelogram and a kite (diagonals, equal opposite angles)
chapters.note: Rare as a separate question; area formulas come under mensuration.

chapters.name: Triangles and Their Properties
learn: Angle bisector theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC (the single most repeated triangle result)
Mid-point theorem: the segment joining two mid-points is half the third side; the medial triangle has half the perimeter and one-fourth the area

Angle between two internal bisectors = 90° + half the third angle; between external bisectors = 90° − half the third angle; angle between the altitude and the bisector = half the difference of the base angles
Angle sum, exterior angle theorem, isosceles and equilateral triangles; height of an equilateral triangle = (√3/2) × side
Pythagoras and its converse: triplets, ladder problems, acute/right/obtuse by comparing squares of sides, 30°-60°-90° ratios
Triangle inequality: range and number of integer values of the third side
Congruence rules (SSS, SAS, RHS) and what they imply
Area ratios: triangles with a common vertex are in the ratio of their bases; a median halves the area
chapters.note: Asked in most papers.

chapters.name: Discount and Marked Price
learn: Chain CP to MP to SP: find the marked price or cost price from the discount% and profit%
Net profit or loss after a mark-up followed by a discount; the mark-up needed for a target profit
Two successive discounts a and b = a + b − ab/100; the single equivalent discount; comparing schemes
Selling price after two successive discounts; find the second discount or the marked price
Discount that cancels a mark-up of m% = m/(100 + m) × 100
"Buy x get y free" = a discount of y/(x + y)
chapters.note: One question in almost every paper; successive discounts are the favourite.

chapters.name: Profit and Loss
learn: SP of x articles = CP of y articles: profit or loss percent
Cost price when the profit at one price equals the loss at another (the mean of the two prices); cost price from the gap between a loss% and a gain% sale
Two articles sold at the same price with equal gain% and loss%: always a net loss of (x²/100)%
Overall profit when parts of the stock are sold at different profit or loss percentages, or part is damaged
Cost price from selling price and profit%, then a new selling price for a target profit
False weights (dishonest dealer), with or without a mark-up
Bought at n for a rupee and sold at m for a rupee; overheads added to cost; profit expressed as a percent of selling price
chapters.note: One question in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Primes, Fractions and Number Basics
learn: Identify primes in a range and test a number for primality (341 = 11 × 31 is not prime)
Count prime factors from the prime factorisation (1024 = 2¹⁰)
Find consecutive (or consecutive even) numbers from their sum
A fraction of a fraction of a number
chapters.note: Mostly from CHSL papers.

chapters.name: Ratio and Proportion
learn: Divide a sum in a given ratio; combine two ratios (A : B and B : C) into a three-term ratio
Ratio before and after adding or removing quantities: find the original numbers or the number to add
Mean proportional √(ab), third proportional b²/a, fourth proportional bc/a
Number to add to or subtract from four terms so they become proportional
Find a : b from a ratio of linear expressions, or from equal fractions or percentages of two quantities
Numbers in a given ratio from the sum of their squares; coins and denominations
chapters.note: One question in most papers.

chapters.name: Average
learn: Find a new, removed or replaced value from the change in average (total = average × count)
Overlapping groups: the common member or the common days from two group averages
Correct an average after a wrongly recorded value; find the number of items from the correction
Combined average of two groups; group size or ratio of groups from the two averages and the combined average
Cricket: batting or bowling average before and after a match, highest score, required run rate
Consecutive and evenly spaced numbers: the average is the middle value; smallest + largest = 2 × average
Average of the first n primes or even numbers; average of squares of the first n naturals = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
chapters.note: One question in most papers.

chapters.name: Compound Interest
learn: Difference between CI and SI for 2 years = P(r/100)² (the most repeated result)
Find the rate from the amounts in two consecutive years, or from principal and amount over 2 years
Half-yearly and quarterly compounding; compounding every 5 or 8 months (adjust the rate and the number of periods)
Compound interest for a fractional number of years
Mixed questions: find the principal or rate from simple interest, then compute compound interest
Divide a sum so that the amounts are equal after different periods; equal annual instalments
chapters.note: About one question in every second paper.

chapters.name: Time and Work
learn: Take total work = LCM of the days and add or subtract daily rates; together time = ab/(a + b)
One worker leaves or joins part-way: find the total time or when the worker left
Working on alternate days
Efficiency ratios and percentages (A is twice as fast as B)
Pairwise times of A, B and C: find all three together or one alone
Man-days: men × days × hours is constant; men, women and boys equivalence; extra workers needed; provisions problems
Wages are shared in the ratio of work done
chapters.note: One question in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Problems on Trains
learn: Crossing a pole: time = train length ÷ speed; crossing a bridge, platform or tunnel: add its length
Two trains: opposite directions add speeds, same direction subtract; distance = sum of lengths
Two trains starting at different times: meeting time and meeting point
Stoppage time per hour from the speeds with and without stoppages

chapters.name: Speed, Time and Distance
learn: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; convert km/h to m/s with 5/18
Chase and meeting problems: time = gap ÷ relative speed, including different start times
Late or early at two speeds: find the distance or the usual time
Change of speed and the resulting time difference (leads to a quadratic); percentage rise in speed to save time
Circular track: first meeting = track length ÷ relative speed; meeting at the start = LCM of lap times
Races: beating by a distance or a time; combining two leads
chapters.note: A question from this chapter or from trains/boats appears in most papers.

chapters.name: Percentage
learn: Price rise and consumption: reduction needed to keep expenditure unchanged = r/(100 + r) × 100; a price cut that buys extra quantity for the same money
Income, expenditure and savings: percentage change in one when the other two change
Chain comparisons: A is x% more than B, B is y% less than C; if A is x% more than B, B as a percent of A
Successive changes: net effect a + b + ab/100; equal rise and fall of r% gives a net fall of r²/100 %; original population
Elections: total votes from turnout, invalid votes and the winning margin
Exams: maximum marks from pass percentage and shortfall; pass or fail percentages of two groups (set formula)
Find a number from the difference of two percentages of it; percentage of a percentage
chapters.note: One question in most papers; price-consumption and income-savings types repeat most.

chapters.name: BODMAS Simplification
learn: Order: brackets, "of", division, multiplication, addition, subtraction; "of" is done before division
Mixed fractions and decimals with nested brackets (bar, round, curly, square)
Find the unknown inside a BODMAS expression
Shortcut with (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b² for near-round products and decimal expressions
chapters.note: Hardly seen before 2019; since then one question in most papers.

chapters.name: Mixture and Alligation
learn: Quantity of water, alcohol or metal to add to reach a target percentage or ratio
Price of a mixture as the weighted average of the component prices; price of one component from the mean price
Rule of alligation to find the mixing ratio for a target concentration or cost
Combined ratio when mixtures with different ratios are mixed
chapters.note: Occasional: about one paper in five.

chapters.name: Cloze Test
learn: A short passage with five blanks, each with four options; read the whole passage once before filling
Most blanks test the noun, verb or adjective that fits the context of the passage
Collocations: plays a vital role, wage a war, took his seat, a study is conducted, flagrant violation, skill development, consists of
Prepositions and phrasal verbs: confined to, derived from, barriers to, looking for, based on, concentrate on
Grammar blanks: subject-verb agreement, keeping the passage tense, articles a/an/the, comparative + than, base verb after a modal
Connectors: however, therefore, moreover, besides, since, as a result, unless, so that
chapters.note: The biggest English block: five questions on one passage in most papers.

chapters.name: Spotting Errors
learn: A sentence is split into parts; find the part with the error, or mark "no error"
Subject-verb agreement: each of / one of the + plural noun / everyone take a singular verb; the verb agrees with the head noun; collective and uncountable nouns (homework, information) are singular
Tense: keep the past consistent in a narrative; past perfect for the earlier of two past actions; for + period, since + point of time
Verb forms: base form after modals, did and to; past participle after has/had/should have and in the passive (bitten, begun, gone)
Prepositions: die of, result in, fond of, excited about, between (two) vs among (many), of vs off
Articles and determiners: the before superlatives and ordinals; a/an by sound; few/many with countable and little/much with uncountable nouns
Pronouns, adjectives and adverbs: who vs which, whose vs who's, each other vs one another; an adverb (well, slowly) modifies a verb, "fastly" is wrong
Redundancy and word choice: returned back, reason ... because, quite too; quiet/quite, further/farther; hardly ... when
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper; subject-verb agreement, tense and prepositions are the three biggest sources.

chapters.name: Sentence Improvement
learn: Replace the underlined part with the best option, or choose "no improvement" (the given sentence is sometimes already correct)
Conditionals: first (if + present, will), third (if + past perfect, would have + past participle), zero; "I wish I were"; "as if" + past
Agreement with pairs: either...or / neither...nor (verb agrees with the nearer subject), as well as (first subject), many a (singular), a gerund subject (singular)
Tense: present perfect continuous with since/for; past perfect before another past event; simple present in a "when" time clause
Comparison: comparative for two, superlative with "of all", "than any other", "one of the + superlative + plural noun", far/by far
Verb patterns: modal + have + past participle, too...to, worth + gerund, gerund after a preposition, fancy + gerund, plan + to-infinitive
Fixed prepositions and phrasal verbs: agree to/with, access to, depend on, wait for vs wait on, put out, break down, cash in on, cut down
Confusable words and pairs: beside/besides, adapt/adopt, few/a few, not only...but also, although vs in spite of; question tags
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Fill in the Blanks
learn: One blank in a sentence; pick the word that fits meaning and grammar
Vocabulary in context is the commonest type: neglected, fragile, malicious, proficient, negligent, confiscated, luxuriant, impenetrable
Collocations: a unanimous decision, render help, a narrow escape, utter confusion, hard-earned money, hold an enquiry, distinguish between
Sound-alike and look-alike words: quiet/quite/quit, dissent/descent, immense/eminent, conscientious/conscious/conscience, loud/laud, flour/floor/flower, scent/sense/cents
Fixed prepositions and phrasal verbs: exempted from, innocent of, engaged in, preside over, fall through, pass down, get along with
Grammar blanks: since + point of time, lay/laid, past perfect, no sooner...than, as...as, question tags
chapters.note: Homophone and confusable-word blanks have become more common in recent papers.

chapters.name: Synonyms
learn: One word given, pick the closest meaning from four options
Recurring words: morose (gloomy), obligatory (mandatory/compulsory), vacillate (waver), chronic (persistent), robust (sturdy), retaliate (strike back), mundane (everyday)
Harder words that were asked: taciturn, lacuna, sagacious, hoodwink, temerity, enervate, munificent, innuendo, perjury, ravenous, livid
Easy words also appear (final, honest, boring, toxic), so do not over-think them
Pick the closest option when no perfect synonym is given
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Antonyms
learn: One word given, pick the opposite from four options; the word is sometimes underlined in a sentence
Know the meaning first: most misses come from hard words such as opprobrium (× adulation), fecund (× sterile), quiescent (× active), obdurate (× amenable), incessant (× sporadic)
Everyday pairs are asked just as often: scarce × plentiful, hostile × amiable, frugal × extravagant, conceal × reveal, transient × permanent
Words that came more than once: sluggish × active, industrious × lethargic/indolent, exonerate
When no exact opposite is offered, choose the nearest one among the options
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper; revise synonyms and antonyms from one word list.

chapters.name: Idioms and Phrases
learn: An idiom is given, usually inside a sentence; pick its meaning
Repeated ones: leave no stone unturned, a hard nut to crack, keep at arm's length, cakewalk, chicken-hearted / lily-livered (cowardly)
Conflict and difficulty: at daggers drawn, bury the hatchet, face the music, bite the bullet, take the bull by the horns, a tight corner, add fuel to the fire
People and behaviour: dark horse, couch potato, apple of one's eye, cat's paw, sit on the fence, pass the buck, blow one's own trumpet

Others asked: a bolt from the blue, the sword of Damocles, Hobson's choice, take French leave, in black and white, through thick and thin, nip in the bud, by leaps and bounds, break a leg, cut corners
Proverb-style items appear in CHSL: a blessing in disguise, actions speak louder than words
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper.

chapters.name: One Word Substitution
learn: A description is given; pick the single word for it
People: teetotaller, philatelist, philanthropist, bibliophile, centenarian, cynic, sceptic, fatalist, pessimist, impostor, invigilator, truant, stevedore
Qualities: ambidextrous, gregarious, omniscient, incorrigible, insatiable, ambivalent, edible, audible/inaudible, feasible, posthumous
Places and things: mint, hangar, dormitory, larder, aquarium, nursery, pillion, harpoon, wreath, graffiti
Studies and practices: entomology, lexicography, numerologist; group words such as fleet, drove, caravan, trilogy
Other repeats: obituary, pseudonym, verbatim, euthanasia, apartheid, abdicate, procrastinate, blasphemy
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper; edible, graffiti and impostor each came twice.

chapters.name: Spelling
learn: Pick the correctly spelt word, or the misspelt word, among four options; newer papers ask for the sentence with no misspelt word
Double letters: commemorate, embarrassment, beginning, association, necessity, acknowledge, millionaire
ie / ei words: niece, receipt, seize, conceive, relieve, perceive, believe, heist
Endings -ance/-ence, -ible/-able, -ous: acquaintance, attendance, interference, contemptible, palatable, surreptitious, erroneous, atrocious, luxurious
Other words asked: connoisseur, renaissance, privilege, calendar, definite, veterinary, restaurant, hierarchical, secretariat, rhyme, diabetes, pursuit
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper; definite, exclamation and luxurious were repeated.

chapters.name: Para Jumbles
learn: Two formats: order four jumbled sentences into a paragraph, or order the jumbled parts of one sentence
Find the opening sentence first: it introduces the topic and has no pronoun or connector pointing backwards
Use connectors as links: however, but, also, therefore, thus, finally, this is because
Follow pronoun references (he, this, these) and pairs such as some ... others
Common orders: general to specific, definition then details, chronological narrative, problem then action then outcome
Some questions fix the first and last sentences and ask only for the middle order
chapters.note: Asked in most papers, often two questions.

chapters.name: Active and Passive Voice
learn: Convert a sentence both ways: active to passive and passive to active
Simple tenses: is/are, was/were, will be + past participle (the simple past is asked most)
Continuous and perfect: is/was being + past participle; has/have/had been + past participle
Modals: could/should be + past participle; has to becomes has to be + past participle
Imperatives: "Let ... be + past participle" or "should be + past participle"; negative imperatives
Questions (By whom is ... being ...?), sentences with two objects, "It is believed that ...", and "nobody" turning into a negative passive
chapters.note: Asked in most papers, usually one or two questions.

chapters.name: Direct and Indirect Speech
learn: Convert direct to indirect speech, and sometimes indirect back to direct
Statements: said to becomes told; tense backshift (present to past, past to past perfect); pronoun changes
Time and place words: now/then, this/that, ago/before, tomorrow/the next day
Questions: yes/no with asked if/whether, wh-questions in statement word order; will becomes would, can becomes could
Commands and requests: told/requested/begged/advised ... (not) to, forbade ... to
Exclamations and wishes: exclaimed with joy/sorrow that, wished/prayed that ... might
No tense change when the reporting verb is in the present or the statement is a universal truth
chapters.note: Exactly one question per paper whenever it appears.

chapters.name: Number Classification
learn: Odd pair where the second is not the same function of the first (n², n² + constant, 3n + 4, n(n + 1), half plus one)
Primes versus composites, perfect squares and cubes, multiples of 5, 7 or 11
Constant difference or ratio between the two numbers of a pair
Triads: third = product of the first two, or a multiple of their sum or difference
Digit patterns: digit sum, reversed digits, last two digits as the square or product of the first
chapters.note: Asked in most papers.

chapters.name: Letter Classification
learn: Odd cluster by the gaps between consecutive letters (constant +3 or +4, or a pattern such as +3, +4, +5)
Opposite-letter pairs (positions adding to 27)
Forward order versus reverse order clusters
Position arithmetic: first + third = middle, or the product of positions
Vowel count or repeated letters
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Word Classification
learn: Odd word by category: spices and an oilseed, organs and an enzyme, wind and percussion instruments, units and an instrument
Odd word by place: cities of one state, countries of one continent, Union Territories versus a city
Odd pair: synonym pairs versus an antonym pair; polygon and number of sides
Odd word by meaning (highest point versus lowest point) or by use
Sports and science based groups: players of one sport, radioactive elements, rainbow colours
chapters.note: Common up to 2021; almost absent from the 2022 to 2024 papers.

chapters.name: Letter Analogy
learn: Every letter shifted by a constant (+5, −4, +6)
A different shift for each position (+4, −3, +2, −1) or shifts that grow by one
Opposite letters: positions add up to 27 (A↔Z, F↔U)
Reverse the cluster, or swap adjacent pairs, and then shift
Letters of a word rearranged in alphabetical order
chapters.note: Learn letter positions 1 to 26 and the opposite-letter pairs by heart.

chapters.name: Number Analogy
learn: Pairs linked by squares and cubes: n : n², n : n³, n² + 1, (n − 1)², (n − 2)³, n : n(n + 1)
Pairs linked by a constant: add or subtract a fixed number, multiply by a fixed number, same ratio
Two-step rules: ×3 + 16, ÷4 + 2, n(n + 3)/2
Triads and sets: third = sum or product of the first two; middle = a function of the outer numbers; fixed successive differences
Newer format: pick the set that follows the same rule as two given sets, operating on whole numbers and not on their digits
Digit-based links: digit sum, product of digits
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper, often two questions.

chapters.name: Word Analogy
learn: Synonym and antonym pairs; degree of intensity (pain : agony)
Part and whole, item and category, member and group
Tool, instrument or organ and its function; quantity and unit; instrument and what it measures
Animal and its sound, young one or group name
Place and activity, person and dwelling, institution and head, sport and playing area
General-knowledge links: dam and river, trophy and sport, memorial and leader, alloy and metal, science and its subject
chapters.note: Some questions need general knowledge, not just vocabulary.

chapters.name: Matrix Coding
learn: Two letter matrices with numbered rows and columns; each letter is written as its row number followed by its column number
Check the options letter by letter and reject at the first mismatch
chapters.note: Asked only in 2016 to 2018 papers; absent from the newer papers.

chapters.name: Letter Coding
learn: Constant shift for every letter (+1, +3, +10, −3)
Alternating or growing shifts (+1, −1; +2, −3, +4, −5; +1, +2, +3)
Opposite letters (A↔Z), sometimes followed by a shift
Reverse the whole word or each half, then shift
Different rules for vowels and consonants (vowels +3, consonants −3; vowel to next vowel)
Swap letters in pairs, or split the word into blocks and rearrange them
chapters.note: Asked in most papers.

chapters.name: Letter-Number Coding
learn: Word coded as the sum (or product) of its letter positions, sometimes plus or times the number of letters
A multiple of the sum: twice or three times the total
Each letter coded as its position, twice or three times its position, or its square
Reverse positions (A = 26, Z = 1); vowels and consonants coded differently
Derive a letter-to-digit table from two coded words and code a third
Word coded by its number of letters
chapters.note: Asked in most papers.

chapters.name: Symbol Substitution
learn: Letters or symbols stand for +, −, × and ÷: replace them and evaluate by BODMAS
The four signs exchange meanings ("+ means ×"): rewrite the expression first, then simplify
chapters.note: Every one of these ends in a BODMAS evaluation, so the order of operations decides the answer.

chapters.name: Coded Equations and Custom Operators
learn: Find the hidden rule behind false-looking equations (digits rearranged, square then append, halve and reverse)
Custom operators defined by examples: a ∗ b = (a + b) × 10, (a − b) × 2
List the possible totals of a set of weights to find the impossible one
chapters.note: Asked only in 2016 to 2018 papers.

chapters.name: Interchange of Signs and Numbers
learn: Which two signs should be interchanged to make the equation correct
Which two numbers (or digits) should be interchanged
Interchange two signs and two numbers together, then check each option with BODMAS
Recent format: interchange the given sign pairs (+ with −, × with ÷) and evaluate the expression
chapters.note: Asked in most papers from 2019 onwards, often two questions.

chapters.name: Direction and Distance
learn: Track a multi-turn walk and give the final direction from the start
Shortest distance from the start using Pythagoras
Final facing direction after left/right or clockwise/anticlockwise turns given in degrees
Two walkers or two routes: position of one relative to the other
Shadow problems (at sunset shadows fall to the east)
chapters.note: In this set it is common in 2016 to 2017 and CHSL papers and thin afterwards.

chapters.name: Dictionary Order
learn: Arrange four or five words as they appear in a dictionary
Words sharing a common prefix: compare letter by letter from the first letter that differs
Variant: name the word that comes at a given position (second, third, last)
chapters.note: Asked in well over half the papers; easy marks.

chapters.name: Word Formation
learn: Which word cannot (or can) be formed from the letters of a given long word
Check that each letter is present and is not used more often than it occurs
chapters.note: Asked only in 2016 to 2018 papers.

chapters.name: Letter Series
learn: Fill the blanks so that a block of letters repeats (a_bc_ab_ type); test each option
Letter-cluster series where each position has its own constant shift (+2, −1, −2)
Single-letter series with constant, alternating, or growing and shrinking gaps, wrapping past Z
Two alternating series merged into one
Clusters with a fixed middle shift and cycling outer letters or vowels
Alphanumeric series: letters and numbers each move by their own step
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper, often two questions: one fill-the-blanks and one cluster series.

chapters.name: Blood Relations
learn: Symbol-coded relations (A + B means A is the mother of B): decode a chain, or pick the expression that gives a stated relation
Pointing-to-a-photograph and introduction statements ("the only son of my grandfather")
Build a family tree from several statements, with couples and two or three generations
Long chains through in-laws (wife's mother's husband's only daughter)
Track gender and generation at every step of the chain
chapters.note: Asked in most papers; the symbol-coded type dominates recent papers.

chapters.name: Syllogism
learn: Two or three statements with two or three conclusions: decide which follow, using Venn diagrams
Conversion: "Some A are B" gives "Some B are A"; "All A are B" gives "Some B are A"; "No A is B" gives "No B is A"
All + All gives All; All + No gives No; Some + All gives Some
No definite conclusion from two "some" statements or two negative statements
Either-or case for a complementary pair of conclusions
Possibility conclusions in newer papers
chapters.note: Asked in almost every paper.

chapters.name: Calendar and Clock
learn: Day of the week for a later date by counting odd days (days ÷ 7, take the remainder)
The year that has the same calendar as a given year (odd days adding up to a multiple of 7)
A clock gaining or losing a fixed time per day
chapters.note: Occasional; nearly all questions are on the calendar.

chapters.name: Venn Diagrams
learn: Overlapping shapes with numbered or lettered regions: read the region common to two shapes but outside the third
Add the regions belonging to exactly two of three sets
Choose the diagram that best shows the relation among three classes
Word problems: "only one set" from three-set data; two-set inclusion-exclusion
chapters.note: The diagram needs a picture, so this chapter is under-counted here: picture-only questions were left out of the source papers.

chapters.name: Order and Ranking
learn: Arrange five or six people by height, age or weight from pairwise comparisons
Deduce ranks from relative-position clues
Assign items to days of the week from positional clues
chapters.note: Rare.

chapters.name: Statement and Conclusions
learn: Which conclusions follow from a given statement
Which assumptions are implicit in a statement
Strong versus weak arguments: a strong argument gives a real reason tied to the issue
chapters.note: Rare, and only in 2016 to 2017 papers.

chapters.name: Plant Tissues and Physiology
learn: Xylem and phloem parts: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma; companion cells belong to phloem
Sclerenchyma (e.g. coconut husk); meristematic versus permanent tissue
Reproduction terms: parthenocarpy, monoecious, ornithophily (pollination by birds)
Photosynthesis and respiration: glycolysis turns glucose into pyruvic acid
Osmosis and imbibition in everyday examples (why honey does not spoil)
chapters.note: Repeats often; xylem and phloem components are the standard question.

chapters.name: Animal Kingdom
learn: Match the animal to its phylum: jellyfish and sea anemone (Cnidaria), spider and ant (Arthropoda), earthworm (Annelida), tapeworm (Platyhelminthes), sea star (Echinodermata)
Body plan terms: bilateral symmetry, levels of organisation, features of chordates
Odd facts: platypus lays eggs, an octopus has three hearts, a bee has five eyes
Reptiles versus amphibians versus mammals; oviparous animals
Common names: Limulus (horseshoe crab), Typhlops (blind snake), Meandrina (brain coral)
chapters.note: The most asked science chapter, in more than one paper in three. Based on NCERT class 11.

chapters.name: Biological Classification and Names
learn: Binomial names: Latin origin; the second word is the species
Kingdoms: Euglena is a protist; Rhizopus and Mucor are fungi
Scientific names of common plants and animals (teak, dog); humans belong to family Hominidae

chapters.name: Cell Biology and Genetics
learn: Cell organelles and their jobs: ribosomes make proteins, Golgi apparatus, plastids
Discoveries: Robert Hooke (cell, 1665), Leeuwenhoek (bacteria)
Plant cell versus animal cell
Terms: totipotency, plasmid, PPLO (smallest cell), binary fission
Full form of DNA; enzymes in daily life
chapters.note: Asked steadily every year.

chapters.name: Human Body Systems
learn: Blood: red cells are made in bone marrow; haemoglobin carries oxygen
Hormones and glands: insulin from the islets of Langerhans; estrogen, progesterone, testosterone
Functional units and parts: nephron (kidney), cerebellum (balance)
Bones: ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), femur
Reproductive organs: ovary, vas deferens

chapters.name: Plant Kingdom
learn: Classes of algae by colour: Chlorophyceae green, Phaeophyceae brown, Rhodophyceae red
Lichen is an alga and a fungus living together
Special plants: Drosera (insect-eating), Eichhornia (water hyacinth), Marchantia (liverwort)
Habit and leaf type: herb, climber, compound leaves of neem

chapters.name: Motion and Laws of Motion
learn: Newton's third law in everyday examples (recoil of a gun)
Distance versus displacement; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
Friction: sliding friction is less than static friction; it produces heat
Scalars and vectors
Kepler's first law: planets move in ellipses
chapters.note: Repeats often; Newton's third law was asked three times.

chapters.name: Sound
learn: Sound needs a medium to travel
Frequency = speed ÷ wavelength; compressions are regions of high pressure
Acoustics is the study of sound

chapters.name: Fluids and Properties of Matter
learn: Pascal's law; buoyancy and viscosity
Density comparisons: water is denser than ice
Evaporation is faster with more heat, wind and surface area, and lower humidity

chapters.name: Nuclear Physics
learn: Fusion (light nuclei join) versus fission
Half-life sums: three-fourths decays in two half-lives
Cadmium rods control a nuclear reactor
Range of the weak nuclear force

chapters.name: Units and Measuring Instruments
learn: SI units: newton (force), pascal (pressure), kelvin (temperature), joule (work), m/s (speed)
Dimensions: impulse has the same dimensions as momentum; electron-volt is a unit of energy
Instruments and what they measure: fathometer (ocean depth), tensiometer, vernier calliper
chapters.note: The most asked physics chapter and the easiest: learn the SI unit table.

chapters.name: Chemical Reactions and Redox
learn: Rusting needs oxygen and moisture and is a redox reaction
Oxidation is loss of electrons; spotting a reaction that is not redox
Types of reaction: combination, decomposition, displacement (zinc with sulphuric acid)
Exothermic versus endothermic changes
First-order reaction
chapters.note: Repeats often; rusting is the usual example.

chapters.name: Atomic Structure and Bonding
learn: Protons, neutrons and electrons; atomic number and mass (lithium has 3 protons; oxygen is 16 u)
Chadwick discovered the neutron (1932)
Isotopes; cations and anions
Atomicity: N2 is diatomic, ozone is O3

chapters.name: Chemical Names and Formulae
learn: Common names: dry ice (solid CO2), baking soda, blue vitriol, Epsom salt, marsh gas, quicklime
Symbols from Latin names: Fe (ferrum), As (arsenic)
Formulae of common compounds and ions: NH4OH, CaO, CN−
chapters.note: Repeats often; dry ice was asked twice.

chapters.name: Chemistry in Everyday Life
learn: What everyday things contain: matchbox (red phosphorus), gunpowder (potassium nitrate), cement (silica), garlic smell (sulphur compounds)
Antacids neutralise stomach acid
Hardness of water: removed by washing soda or zeolite
Fertiliser types: superphosphate is phosphatic

chapters.name: Metals and Non-Metals
learn: Metalloids: boron, silicon, antimony
Unusual metals: mercury is liquid, potassium is soft
Alloys and uses: galinstan replaces mercury in thermometers; copper kills bacteria

chapters.name: Diseases and Vaccines
learn: Disease and its cause: chickenpox (varicella zoster virus), Ebola and AIDS (viruses), Minamata (mercury), diabetes (low insulin), haemophilia (blood does not clot)
Communicable versus non-communicable diseases
Faecal-oral spread: the "F-diagram" (fluids, fields, flies, fingers, food); what a fomite is
Tests and vaccines: Widal test for typhoid, BCG for tuberculosis
Organ affected: glaucoma (optic nerve), epilepsy (brain)
chapters.note: Asked in about one paper in four.

chapters.name: Vitamins and Nutrition
learn: Deficiency diseases: vitamin A (night blindness), vitamin K (blood does not clot)
Food sources of vitamins (milk is poor in vitamin C)

chapters.name: Networking, Internet and Databases
learn: Protocols and their layer: HTTP (application), TCP (transport), IP (network)
HTML makes web pages; scripting languages for the web
Databases: primary key, SQL
chapters.note: Asked only in older papers (2016 to 2018).

chapters.name: Computer Fundamentals
learn: Memory: ROM is permanent; 4 bits make a nibble
Operating systems (Linux, Windows) versus programming languages
Terms and full forms: bug, ISDN
MS Word basics
chapters.note: Asked only in older papers (2016 to 2018).

chapters.name: Scientists, Inventions and Discoveries
learn: Inventor and invention: Fleming (penicillin), Maiman (laser), Janssen (microscope), Einthoven (ECG), Eli Whitney (cotton gin), de Mestral (Velcro)
Physics names: J. J. Thomson (electron), Celsius and Kelvin (temperature scales), Einstein (relativity)
Instruments and who invented them: seismometer, barograph, telegraph
Nobel firsts in science and nationality of scientists
chapters.note: Asked in about one paper in four; heavy in 2017 and 2019 papers, with some very obscure inventors.

chapters.name: Books and Authors
learn: Books by national leaders: Nehru (Glimpses of World History), Azad (India Wins Freedom), Ambedkar (The Buddha and His Dhamma)
Hindi and Bengali classics: Kamayani (Jaishankar Prasad), Anandamath (Bankim Chandra), Nil Darpan (Dinabandhu Mitra)
Indian English writers: Jhumpa Lahiri, Amitav Ghosh, Vikram Seth, V. S. Naipaul
Books released in the last year and memoirs of celebrities and sportspersons
Booker Prize winner of the year
chapters.note: The most asked static GK chapter, in nearly half the papers. Mix of classics and books from the last year.

chapters.name: Festivals and Fairs of India
learn: Match the festival to its state: Gangaur and Pushkar Fair (Rajasthan), Hemis (Ladakh), Thaipusam and Puthandu (Tamil Nadu), Lathmar Holi (Uttar Pradesh), Phool Dei (Uttarakhand)
Lesser-known fairs: Madhavpur Mela (Gujarat), Poush Mela (Santiniketan), Rottela Panduga (Andhra Pradesh), Kullu Dussehra (Himachal Pradesh)
What the festival marks: Baisakhi (founding of the Khalsa), Durga Puja
Month or occasion of a festival
chapters.note: Repeats very often, mostly since 2022: about two papers in five.

chapters.name: Indian Culture, Tribes and Languages
learn: Martial arts and their state: Mardani Khel (Maharashtra), Lathi (Punjab and West Bengal)
Gurdwaras and monasteries and where they are (Hemkund Sahib, Namdroling)
Crafts, languages and tribes by state: Chikankari (Lucknow), Bodo (Assam), Nyishi (Arunachal Pradesh)
National symbols of neighbouring countries

chapters.name: Classical Dances of India
learn: Dance and its state: Sattriya (Assam), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Kathak (North India)
Famous exponents: Kelucharan Mohapatra (Odissi), Rukmini Devi Arundale and Mrinalini Sarabhai (Bharatanatyam)
Technical terms: Alarippu, nattuvanar and Vazhuvoor style (Bharatanatyam), Kalasam (Kathakali)
chapters.note: A top static GK chapter from 2022 onwards, with questions on dancers and technical terms.

chapters.name: Musicians, Artists and Instruments
learn: Musician and instrument: Amjad Ali Khan and Ali Akbar Khan (sarod), Vilayat Khan (sitar), Sultan Khan (sarangi), Hariprasad Chaurasia (flute), Zakir Hussain (tabla), Vishwa Mohan Bhatt (Mohan Veena)
Vocalists and film music names: Bhimsen Joshi, Lata Mangeshkar, R. D. Burman
Painters: M. F. Husain and his horses, Picasso
Gharanas, vocal forms and festivals: Bishnupur gharana (Dhrupad), Tappa (Punjab), Tansen Samaroh (Gwalior)
chapters.note: Asked in about one paper in three; instrument-player pairs dominate recent papers.

chapters.name: Sportspersons and Their Sports
learn: Match the player to the sport: Deepika Kumari and Limba Ram (archery), Manika Batra (table tennis), Fouaad Mirza (equestrian), Nethra Kumanan (sailing)
chapters.note: Asked in about one paper in seven; less famous sports are favoured.

chapters.name: Olympics, Asian and National Games
learn: Olympic basics: five rings; Summer and Winter Games are two years apart
India's hockey golds (last in 1980 at Moscow)
Asian Games are held every four years; India's best sport there is athletics
Hosts of past National Games

chapters.name: Firsts in India
learn: First women: Governor (Sarojini Naidu), Chief Minister (Sucheta Kripalani)
First Governors and Chief Ministers of states
First winners of awards (Filmfare, Bhatnagar Prize, Indian woman Grammy winner)
Other firsts: first commercial pilot (J. R. D. Tata), first golf club (Kolkata)

chapters.name: Superlatives and Records
learn: Longest-serving Chief Minister and Governor
World records: smallest bird, Guinness records held by Indians
Unique places such as the floating post office on Dal Lake

chapters.name: Solar System and Earth's Motions
learn: Order of the planets; Venus is the hottest; Pluto is a dwarf planet
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun
Solstices and equinoxes: 21 June is the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere; the Sun is overhead at the Equator twice a year
Theories of origin: nebular hypothesis (Laplace), steady state theory (Fred Hoyle)
chapters.note: Repeats often, with very easy questions.

chapters.name: Soils and Soil Erosion
learn: Types of erosion: sheet erosion is the least visible; badlands form from gully erosion
Conservation methods: shelter belts, mulching
Humus is decayed organic matter in soil

chapters.name: Pollution
learn: Acid rain is caused by oxides of nitrogen and sulphur; smog contains VOCs, nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide
Water quality measures: dissolved oxygen, BOD measured over 5 days
Thermal pollution comes from hot water released by power plants
Solid waste disposal methods: landfill, composting, incineration
Aerosols, DDT in soil and water, air-cleaning devices (bag filters, scrubbers)
chapters.note: Asked mostly in 2016 and 2017 papers.

chapters.name: Ecology and Ecosystem
learn: Who coined what: Haeckel "ecology", Tansley "ecosystem"; E. P. Odum is the father of modern ecology
Terms: synecology, carrying capacity, eurythermal, brood parasitism
Steps of decomposition: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation

chapters.name: National Parks and Wildlife
learn: Match the park or sanctuary to its state: Bhitarkanika (Odisha), Borail (Assam), Baghmara Pitcher Plant Sanctuary (Meghalaya), Campbell Bay (Great Nicobar)
Flagship species: Kanha for swamp deer (barasingha)
Project Tiger began in 1973
Number of national parks in India

chapters.name: Agriculture and Crops
learn: Local names of shifting cultivation: Jhum in the north-east, Kuruwa in Jharkhand
Crop and soil pairs: rice on alluvial soil, cashew on red laterite soil
Top producing states (Madhya Pradesh for pulses)
Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon and harvested in September-October
Jowar is the main food crop of semi-arid central and southern India

chapters.name: Dams and River Projects
learn: Match the dam to its river and state: Hirakud (Mahanadi, Odisha), Jayakwadi (Godavari, Maharashtra), Ukai (Tapi, Gujarat), Almatti (Krishna), Koteshwar (Bhagirathi)
Bhakra is the highest gravity dam in India
chapters.note: Always the same question type: which river is the dam on.

chapters.name: States and Cities of India
learn: Which states border a given state
Nicknames and twin cities: Madurai "Athens of the East", Hubli-Dharwad
Tourist places and their state (Araku Valley, Andhra Pradesh)
Relative north-south position of major cities

chapters.name: India's Borders and Neighbours
learn: Boundary lines: Radcliffe Line (India-Pakistan); Siachen dispute
India's longest border is with Bangladesh
Which neighbours are landlocked (Nepal, Bhutan, Afghanistan) and which are not (Myanmar)
Basic facts about neighbours: Bangladesh borders only India and Myanmar; rice is Sri Lanka's chief crop

chapters.name: Soils and Natural Vegetation
learn: Black soil: holds moisture, cracks when dry, found on the Deccan trap, poor in phosphorus
Red soil forms on crystalline rocks in low-rainfall parts of the Deccan
Forest types and typical trees: teak in tropical deciduous, sundari in mangroves, conifers in the Himalaya
Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover by area
Forest products such as tendu leaves for bidis

chapters.name: World Oceans, Rivers and Canals
learn: The Amazon is the largest river, in South America (Brazil)
Which ocean an island or sea belongs to: Madagascar in the Indian Ocean; the Black Sea is linked to the Atlantic
The Suez Canal is about 193 km long

chapters.name: Mughal and Indo-Islamic Architecture
learn: Builder of each monument: Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan), Agra Fort (Akbar), Bibi Ka Maqbara (Azam Shah)
Akbar's tomb is at Sikandra; Panch Mahal is at Fatehpur Sikri
Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur has the largest dome in India

chapters.name: Monuments and Heritage Sites
learn: Who built what and where: Charminar (Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, Hyderabad), Konark Sun Temple (Narasimhadeva I)
Buddhist sites: Sanchi stupa, Ghoom Monastery (Darjeeling)
Caves: Elephanta (Maharashtra), Lomas Rishi in the Barabar Hills (Bihar)
Modern and colonial buildings: Victoria Terminus, Open Hand Monument by Le Corbusier
Mathura school of sculpture in the Kushana period
chapters.note: Asked in about one paper in five.

chapters.name: Philosophy and Cultural Institutions
learn: Founders of schools of philosophy: Kanada (Vaisheshika), Charvaka (Lokayata)
Shantiniketan: founded by Rabindranath Tagore in 1901; Kala Bhavana is its art school

chapters.name: Early Medieval Kingdoms and Cholas
learn: Dynasty, founder and capital: Rashtrakutas (Dantidurga, Malkhed), Pratiharas (Kannauj), Pallavas (Kanchi), Senas (Lakhnauti)
Chola village assemblies: Sabha for Brahmana villages, Ur for ordinary villages; shalabhoga land for schools
Palas: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and supported Nalanda
Terms: samanta, nagara-shreshthi

chapters.name: Medieval Literature and Travellers
learn: Chand Bardai wrote Prithviraj Raso
Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind

chapters.name: Mughal Empire
learn: Babur and the Battle of Khanwa (1527) against Rana Sanga and his allies
Humayun regained Delhi in 1555; Sher Shah's administration was the model for Akbar
Akbar: Bairam Khan, Todar Mal's zabti revenue system, Ain-i-Akbari, tomb at Sikandra
Jahangir: earlier Prince Salim, wife Nur Jahan, Sir Thomas Roe at his court
Aurangzeb died in 1707; court chronicles were written in Persian
chapters.note: The most asked history chapter; the Battle of Khanwa came up three times.

chapters.name: British Conquest and Battles
learn: Battle of Plassey, 1757: East India Company against Siraj-ud-Daulah
Third Battle of Panipat, 1761; Battle of Saragarhi, 1897
Awadh was annexed in 1856 (last Nawab Wajid Ali Shah)
Lahore was the capital of Maharaja Ranjit Singh

chapters.name: Post-Independence India
learn: Liberation of Goa from the Portuguese, 1961
1971 war: Sam Manekshaw was Army Chief
Lahore Declaration, 1999 (Vajpayee's bus journey)
Foreign leaders' first visits and other landmark events after 1947

chapters.name: Socio-Religious Reform Movements
learn: Raja Ram Mohan Roy: Atmiya Sabha (1814), Brahmo Samaj (1828)
Founder and organisation: Arya Samaj (Dayanand Saraswati), Prarthana Samaj (Atmaram Pandurang, 1867), Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan), Theosophical Society (Annie Besant)
Ramakrishna Mission and Belur Math (Vivekananda)
Reformers of Maharashtra: Jyotiba and Savitribai Phule
Parsi reform: Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (Dadabhai Naoroji)
chapters.note: Repeats often. Learn founder, organisation and year together.

chapters.name: Ancient Literature, Science and Education
learn: Books and authors: Arthashastra (Kautilya), Ashtadhyayi (Panini), Mricchakatika (Sudraka)
Scientists: Aryabhata (astronomy), Varahamihira, Charaka (medicine), Sushruta (surgery)
Universities: Takshashila, Nalanda (Bihar), Vikramshila (founded by Dharmapala)
The Vikrama Era began in 57 BC
chapters.note: Asked steadily, almost always as a book-author or scholar-field match.

chapters.name: World History
learn: French Revolution gave the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity
World War I began in 1914
Mesopotamians wrote in cuneiform on clay tablets
chapters.note: Rarely asked in SSC.

chapters.name: Laws, Courts and Committees
learn: Key provision of Bills and Acts passed in the last year (e.g. Election Laws Amendment Act 2021: four qualifying dates for voter enrolment)
High Court and Supreme Court rulings that were in the news
Committees in the news and who headed them (e.g. Afzal Amanullah Committee on Haj subsidy)
chapters.note: Mostly current affairs: follow the last 12 months.

chapters.name: National Events and Projects
learn: Inaugurations of big projects: Atal Tunnel, Kartarpur Corridor, largest plants and tunnels, and the state they are in
Renamed places, e.g. Havelock Island became Swaraj Dweep
New trains and railway initiatives
Conferences held in India and their themes
First-of-its-kind festivals and events in states and UTs
chapters.note: Mostly current affairs: follow the last 12 months.

chapters.name: Reports, Indices and Rankings
learn: India's rank in the latest global indices: Human Development Index, Global Innovation Index, Travel and Tourism Competitiveness
Which body publishes which report: UNDP (HDI), IEA (World Energy Outlook), UNEP (Food Waste Index), IQAir (air quality)
Top-ranked country or city in each index
NITI Aayog indices such as the Multidimensional Poverty Index (Bihar was the poorest state in the first one)
Rich lists and philanthropy lists (Hurun)
chapters.note: Asked steadily. Learn the report, its publisher and India's latest rank as one unit.

chapters.name: International Awards and Titles
learn: Oscar winners of the year in the main acting categories
Global prizes with their latest winner: Templeton Prize, Global Teacher Prize, World Press Photo, Joan Miro Prize
International honours given to Indian leaders, e.g. Global Goalkeeper Award for Swachh Bharat
Miss Universe and Miss World winners, including the list of Indian winners
chapters.note: Mostly current affairs: follow the last 12 months.

chapters.name: Olympics and Multi-Sport Games
learn: Host cities of upcoming and recent Olympics, Paralympics and Asian Games
India's results at the latest Olympics, including the hockey matches
National Games: host state and top medal winners (36th Games in Gujarat, 2022)
Khelo India Youth Games venue
Sports added to or dropped from the Games
chapters.note: Mostly current affairs: follow the last 12 months.

chapters.name: Central Government Schemes
learn: Aim and target year of each new scheme (Jal Jeevan Mission: tap water to every rural home by 2024)
The ministry or body that runs it (DACE: Social Justice ministry; Ubharte Sitaare Fund: Exim Bank and SIDBI)
First states to achieve a scheme target (Goa, then Telangana, for 100% tap connections)
Full forms and components: PM-WANI, NAMASTE, NDEAR, SAMPANN
Duration of extended schemes, e.g. Samagra Shiksha 2.0 runs 2021 to 2026
chapters.note: Asked in nearly one paper in three. Jal Jeevan Mission alone was asked several times.

chapters.name: Science and Technology News
learn: Venue of the latest Indian Science Congress
New science initiatives and who launched them (e.g. I-STEM's WEST for women in science)
Headline science projects abroad of the year
chapters.note: Rarely asked. Follow the last 12 months.

chapters.name: Emergency Provisions
learn: The President proclaims an emergency
Parliament must approve a national emergency within one month

chapters.name: Forms of Government
learn: Three organs: legislature, executive, judiciary
Presidential versus parliamentary system
The United Kingdom has no written constitution
Pressure groups try to influence policy; they do not contest elections

chapters.name: Making of the Constitution
learn: Constituent Assembly committees and their chairmen; the Drafting Committee had seven members
Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution; the National Anthem was adopted on 24 January 1950
Borrowed features: Directive Principles (Ireland), Fundamental Duties (USSR), independent judiciary (USA)
chapters.note: Repeats often. One 2022 shift asked several detailed Constituent Assembly questions.

chapters.name: Parliament
learn: Parliament is the President plus both Houses (Article 79); quorum is one-tenth (Article 100)
Rajya Sabha: six-year term, seats by state under the Fourth Schedule (Article 80)
Money Bills: the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes; a bill becomes an Act with the President's assent
Speaker decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule
Public Accounts Committee examines CAG reports
No-confidence motion; vote on account; sessions of Parliament
chapters.note: The most asked polity chapter, in more than one paper in four.

chapters.name: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
learn: Order and tenures of Prime Ministers: Charan Singh followed Morarji Desai; shortest tenures (Gulzarilal Nanda, Chandra Shekhar)
No limit on the number of terms a Prime Minister can serve

chapters.name: Governor and State Legislature
learn: Governor takes the oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court
One Governor can serve two or more states (7th Amendment)
A Money Bill in a state assembly needs the Governor's recommendation

chapters.name: Judiciary and Writs
learn: The five writs and their use: quo warranto (right to hold office), prohibition (stops a lower court)
Writ powers: Article 32 (Supreme Court), Article 226 (High Courts)
Supreme Court decisions bind all courts
Removal of judges: Justice V. Ramaswami faced the first impeachment motion
Malimath Committee on criminal justice reform

chapters.name: Fundamental Rights
learn: Article numbers: 14 to 18 (equality), 19 (freedoms), 20, 21 (life and liberty), 22 (arrest), 24 (child labour)
Right to Property was removed by the 44th Amendment
Recent Supreme Court readings, e.g. internet access under Article 19
chapters.note: Asked as "which Article deals with...". Learn Articles 12 to 35 by number.

chapters.name: Demand, Supply and Types of Goods
learn: Normal, inferior and Giffen goods: how demand moves with income and price
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable; private goods are rival and excludable
Derived demand: demand for a factor of production comes from demand for the final good
Movement along a curve (expansion or contraction) versus a shift of the curve; equilibrium price
Price elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price
chapters.note: Among the most repeated economics chapters; inferior and normal goods come up again and again.

chapters.name: Economic Terms and Thinkers
learn: Barter: goods themselves act as the medium of exchange
Marginal propensity to consume lies between 0 and 1
Terms: Golden Handshake (voluntary retirement scheme), trickle-down theory, income as a flow
Economists: Keynes (England, Keynesian economics), Haberler (opportunity cost theory of trade)

chapters.name: Inflation
learn: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level
Core inflation leaves out food and energy prices
Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − inflation rate

chapters.name: National Income
learn: Three methods of measuring national income: product, income and expenditure
GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP (also called the implicit price deflator)
Depreciation is consumption of fixed capital
GDP at market prices versus factor cost (taxes and subsidies); how personal income is derived from national income
Definition of GDP and what its sector-wise split shows
chapters.note: Definitions and formulas repeat; the three measurement methods were asked more than once.

chapters.name: Financial Markets and Payments
learn: Bombay Stock Exchange was founded in 1875 by Premchand Roychand
Regulators: the Forward Markets Commission regulated commodity futures (now merged with SEBI)
Payment terms: merchant discount rate, the 22-character UTR number in RTGS
Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019

chapters.name: Exchange Rate and Balance of Payments
learn: Devaluation lowers a currency's value: exports get cheaper, imports costlier
Real exchange rate and the Purchasing Power Parity theory
Balance of Payments records all transactions with the rest of the world
